title: Strain-tuned orbital-dependent electronic correlations in FeTe thin films
authors: Hyunjee Song, Sangjae Lee, Keun-Yeol Park, Jaehyun Park, Suyoung Lee, Yeonjae Lee, Jinyoung Kim, Jaeung Lee, Celesta S. Chang, Younsik Kim, Changyoung Kim
abstract: Iron chalcogenides exhibit rich phenomena which are governed by orbital-dependent electronic interactions and strong electronic correlation. In particular, many studies have explored orbital selectivity in FeTe through Se doping. Here, applying tensile strain to thin films allows us to precisely control the system without other impurities that may arise from chemical doping to investigate the emergent behaviors in FeTe. Using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we observe a spectral weight transfer between $d_{\rm xy}$ and $d_{\rm z^{2}}$ orbitals, evidence of an orbital-selective Mott phase (OSMP). Beyond OSMP, we reveal hitherto unobserved strain-induced effects, distinct from chemical doping. The evolution of $d_{\rm xz}$ orbital demonstrates how electron hopping mechanism plays an important role in defining the electronic properties of the system. Our findings highlight a direct correlation between epitaxial strain and the evolution of electronic structures in FeTe.
summary: This paper uses ARPES on strained FeTe thin films to study orbital-dependent electronic correlations. By applying tensile strain, the researchers observe evidence of an Orbital-Selective Mott Phase breakdown and map out how lattice deformation specifically controls the coherence of different orbitals like $d_{xz}$. The findings establish a direct link between epitaxial strain and the fundamental electronic structure governing these correlated materials.
main_problem: The study investigates how orbital-dependent electronic correlations in FeTe thin films are tuned by applying epitaxial tensile strain, aiming to separate structural effects from those caused by chemical doping.
main_result: Tensile strain induces an Orbital-Selective Mott Phase (OSMP) breakdown and causes a measurable spectral weight transfer between $d_{xy}$ and $d_{z^2}$ orbitals. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that lattice deformation specifically controls the coherence of the $d_{xz}$ orbital via changes in $	ext{Fe–Fe}$ hopping.
method: The primary technique used is Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES), complemented by structural characterization using RHEED and STEM to monitor strain relaxation as a function of film thickness.
model_or_system: The system under study is FeTe thin films grown epitaxially on substrates, which allows for systematic tuning of lattice parameters via tensile strain. The physics revolves around orbital-dependent electronic interactions characteristic of iron chalcogenides.
key_observables: Spectral weight transfer between $d_{xy}$ and $d_{z^2}$ orbitals; evolution of the $d_{z^2}$ band near the Fermi level; spectral weight ratio changes in the $d_{xz}$ orbital; effective mass evolution for specific orbitals.
important_parameters: Tensile strain magnitude, film thickness (which correlates with strain relaxation), and temperature are the key tuning parameters.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that ARPES can accurately probe subtle changes in electronic structure related to correlation physics, and that the structural control offered by epitaxial strain allows for a clean decoupling of lattice effects from chemical doping.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate thickness-dependent band dispersions ($\Gamma-	ext{X}$ cuts) showing orbital evolution; spectral weight ratios tracking strain relaxation; and schematic diagrams detailing how hopping mechanisms are suppressed or enhanced under tensile versus relaxed strain conditions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents evidence across multiple measurements: first, demonstrating OSMP breakdown via $d_{xy}/d_{z^2}$ transfer due to strain; second, analyzing the thickness dependence of $d_{xz}$ orbital coherence and spectral weight; and finally, proposing a mechanism where lattice deformation directly modulates hopping pathways for specific orbitals.
why_interesting: The work provides an experimental demonstration of how structural parameters (lattice constant) can act as a clean tuning knob to manipulate strong electronic correlations in correlated materials, offering insights applicable to designing quantum materials.
